title: JDTLS batch file fails when located in a folder path with spaces
body_truncated:
I'm a Windows user. I recently unpacked the latest JDTLS zip file into my user directory. When I tried to run JDTLS from the command prompt (after adding it to my PATH), I got the following error:

```
C:\Users\Thomas Kain\Desktop>jdtls
C:\Users\Thomas Kain\AppData\Local\Python\pythoncore-3.14-64\python.exe: can't open file 'C:\\Users\\Thomas': [Errno 2] No such file or directory
Press any key to continue . . .
```

This error seemingly occurs because my user directory has spaces in its name and JDTLS's batch startup script on Windows isn't handling that correctly. For reference, here is `jdtls.bat` as it is included with [JDTLS 1.50.0](https://projects.eclipse.org/projects/eclipse.jdt.ls/releases/1.50.0):

```bat
@echo off
python %~dp0/jdtls %*
pause
```

Simply adding quotes around `%~dp0/jdtls` seems to fix the issue for me.

Projects that reference `${maven.multiModuleProjectDirectory}` in their POM (e.g., Apache Dubbo, Google Guava) fail to import. The Maven CLI launcher (`mvn`) normally sets this as a JVM system property via `-Dmaven.multiModuleProjectDirectory=...`, but JDTLS does not replicate this behavior.

title: Unreliable Maven artifact search
body_truncated:
I faced an issue, with JDTLS not showing sources for multiple classes of OSS dependencies. Digging a bit deeper, it seems that the root cause is outside JDTLS - the `search.maven.org` doesn't return results for correct hashes.

For example, I tried Spring Boot:
* Given the correct hash of 3.5.4: https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/springframework/boot/spring-boot/3.5.4/spring-boot-3.5.4.jar.sha1

title: Early log messages are not filtered
body_truncated: In `LogHandler.java` status objects obtained from the log listener can be filtered by a predicate. The filter cannot be applied to those mesages. My suggestion would be to convert the filter to filter `LogEntry` objects and to convert `IStatus` objects into `LogEntry` before filtering.

title: Syntax errors in WorkspaceDiagnosticsHandlerTest
body_truncated:
I noticed a while ago that something weird was going on with the semantic tokens in some of the test cases in `WorkspaceDiagnosticsHandlerTest`:

![image](https://github.com/eclipse/eclipse.jdt.ls/assets/52179873/d81fb620-b0ff-4b3d-a41b-fad836816c98)

And also, `projectDiags` is being marked as "not used", which is strange.

Initially I thought this was just a bug in the semantic tokens handler (or something to do with the AST), and decided that I would investigate it later when I had more time. But then yesterday, I updated vscode-java from version `1.18.0` to `1.19.0`, and now I get a syntax error:

![syntax-error](https://github.com/eclipse/eclipse.jdt.ls/assets/52179873/20b9d104-1c98-4fe8-8ee3-21700f9093c1)

And indeed, there is a syntax error (two, actually) in `WorkspaceDiagnosticsHandlerTest`! I just couldn't believe it at first: Why would the compiler not reject such code, and why would the tests not fail?

After some digging (remember, the syntax error is only reported by vscode-java >= `1.19.0`...), I believe I've found the root cause, a bug in ECJ: eclipse-jdt/eclipse.jdt.core#367. This bug was fixed by eclipse-jdt/eclipse.jdt.core#1047, which made its way into vscode-java `1.19.0`.

But why do the test cases still not fail? As far as I understand, that's just because they are compiled by tycho-compiler-plugin, and JDT LS currently uses tycho `3.0.4` which uses ECJ `3.33.0` (see https://github.com/eclipse-tycho/tycho/blob/tycho-3.0.4/pom.xml#L89) which is an older version that doesn't contain eclipse-jdt/eclipse.jdt.core#1047.

Before that bug fix, ECJ would simply ignore the rest of the method (after the syntax error), but still compile all the statements before the syntax error (without rejecting the code). This meant that the test cases would never fail, because they were in fact mostly empty (most of the assert calls were ignored by ECJ, since they occurred after the syntax error).

title: Diagnostics from changes to build configuration not reflected in open source files
body_truncated:
This is a regression from https://github.com/eclipse/eclipse.jdt.ls/pull/1930#issuecomment-985920473 . The motivation behind that change was to prevent a race condition by ensuring a file's diagnostics are handled either by the `WorkspaceDiagnosticsHandler` or the `BaseDiagnosticsHandler`, but not both.

However, if a change is made to something like `java.configuration.runtimes`, the `WorkspaceDiagnosticsHandler` will report the errors, and completely ignore opened files as they should be handled by `BaseDiagnosticsHandler` . The diagnostics won't be reflected in the opened file until the next time it is modified.

title: Cached decompiled content served indefinitely even though source is available
body_truncated:
See https://github.com/redhat-developer/vscode-java/issues/447

Basically if the source file was not attached at some point and the decompiled content was served, even after the source is attached, the cached decompiled version keeps being served.

After looking into evicting the ContentProviderManager cache on classpath change, I came to realize this whole caching strategy implementation was a mistake in the 1st place. Caching is good for slow decompilers, BUT, caching should be an implementation detail of the IContentProvider. For instance if say the FernDecompiler is slow, it should cache its own entries. Changing `java.contentProvider.preferred` would serve the appropriate content, cached or not, as per each provider implementation.

So, I plan on removing Cache<String, String> cachedContent from ContentProviderManager, and deprecating cacheable from https://github.com/eclipse/eclipse.jdt.ls/blob/0a792b21042c121499d6052a93346c348e95c475/org.eclipse.jdt.ls.core/schema/org.eclipse.jdt.ls.core.contentProvider.exsd#L83

Eventually, each provider will be responsible for caching their results, should it be necessary.

title: completion request should include textEdit according to protocol
body_truncated:
The current version of the protocol contains the [following text](https://github.com/Microsoft/language-server-protocol/blob/master/protocol.md#completion-request):

> However, properties that are needed for the inital sorting and filtering, like sortText, filterText, insertText, and textEdit must be provided in the textDocument/completion request and must not be changed during resolve.

However jdt.ls returns only `insertText` in the original response, but then adds a `textEdit` after a resolve. This is a strict violation of the protocol and in editors that can't handle the resolve request properly, requires either that we resolve every completion item (the use of textEdit is not optional, [insertion text alone doesn't work for things like imports](https://github.com/eclipse/eclipse.jdt.ls/issues/353)).

Is it possible to include the `textEdit` in the initial response?

title: InitializeParams#rootPath is ignored
body_truncated:
According to [Language Server Protocol 3.0](https://github.com/Microsoft/language-server-protocol/blob/3.0.0/protocol.md#initialize) InitializeParams contains both a `rootPath` (though deprecated) and `rootUri` (preferred). Both of these are supported [in LSP4J](https://github.com/eclipse/lsp4j/blob/3c309e0fe63056bb8146c104774c0ebb2112cb58/org.eclipse.lsp4j/src/main/xtend-gen/org/eclipse/lsp4j/InitializeParams.java#L77).

In pre-0.1.0 versions of eclipse.jdt.ls, both `getRootPath` and `getRootUri` were checked (see [this commit](https://github.com/eclipse/eclipse.jdt.ls/commit/277ee177090843c0b2560e779d3bff3af9dd9ce5#diff-77a4e07ecb50e4529272a8d107e6c143) for when this changed).

This presents as an issue in Atom where ide-java, relying on atom-languageclient, is sending initialize calls with a `rootPath` only. I'm opening a ticket with them to resolve this, but having eclipse.jdt.ls support both `getRootPath` and `getRootUri` would comply better with the spec.

See atom/ide-java#37 for resulting error.

body_truncated:
So the server fails to start 95% of the time when started with the -noverify flag, and rarely succeeds, which smells like a race condition.

After some tracing, I found that, when the server is started the following happens:
- LanguageServer application is accessed on main thread
- it triggers JavaLanguageServerPlugin start(), which starts the JavaClientConnection which spawns some other Thread(s)
- the Initialization handler is called before above start() ends from an LSP Thread, which NPEs on JavaLanguageServerPlugin.getLanguageServer().setParentProcessId(...); because the language server hasn't been set
- JavaLanguageServerPlugin start() has finished, the LanguageServer is set on JavaLanguageServerPlugin the main thread. Too late.
